## Vocabulary

- **self**: Liquidation price math for looped positions (5/2)

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] Interest accrual moves the liquidation price while the position is open. Kamino's example is a $7,000 USDC debt at a 10% borrow rate with flat prices, which drifts from 70% LTV to 77% over 12 months. For a LST/SOL loop the drift equals borrow cost minus staking yield on the leveraged balance: it is upward only when the spread is negative. A static liquidation price quoted at entry is therefore stale after entry. (medium confidence) — https://kamino.com/docs/products/borrow/concepts · keywords: Liquidation price math for looped positions · also: https://kamino.com/docs/products/multiply/concepts

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Kamino applies a borrow factor to debt: borrow capacity = collateral value x Max LTV / borrow factor. A factor of 2.0 doubles the effective risk-adjusted LTV for the same real debt, so a position can be closer to liquidation than the raw market-value LTV suggests. A liquidation price computed from raw values needs the borrow factor applied to debt. (low confidence) — https://kamino.com/docs/products/borrow/concepts · keywords: Liquidation price math for looped positions

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] For SOL-denominated LST loops (JitoSOL, mSOL, bSOL, JupSOL against SOL debt) Kamino prices the LST by stake rate, LST price = SOL_staked / LST_minted, not by DEX price. Both sides move with SOL, so LTV does not change with SOL's USD price. The liquidation variable is therefore the exchange rate plus the yield-versus-borrow spread. A market discount, such as JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL, does not raise reported LTV. Stake-rate pricing does not protect against a real loss of staked SOL (exploit, slashing), which lowers the exchange rate itself. (medium confidence) — https://kamino.com/docs/products/multiply/concepts · keywords: Liquidation price math for looped positions · also: https://kamino.com/docs/risk/asset-risk/depeg
- [statement] For LST/SOL loops the liquidation variable is the LST exchange rate plus the borrow-versus-yield spread, not SOL's dollar price. Kamino prices LSTs at the stake rate, LST price = SOL_staked / LST_minted, which rises each epoch, so a DEX discount (its example: JitoSOL at 0.95 SOL) does not change LTV. Jupiter Lend pegged vaults price on an on-chain exchange or redemption rate, and its docs add that a drop in that rate (slashing, or a loss in the underlying strategy) can also bring a position to liquidation. Both vendors say stake-rate pricing removes market-noise liquidations but not a real loss of backing. The on-chain oracle configuration of these reserves was not verified in this pass. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06) — https://kamino.com/docs/security/oracles/lst-oracles · keywords: Liquidation price math for looped positions · also: https://kamino.com/docs/products/multiply/concepts, https://docs.jup.ag/user-docs/earn/lend/protocol-details

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Aave defines Health Factor = (Total Collateral Value x Weighted Average Liquidation Threshold) / Total Borrow Value; HF below 1 permits liquidation. The liquidation threshold is set per collateral asset by Aave governance. For a single collateral asset whose debt price is fixed, setting HF = 1 and solving gives liquidation price = debt / (collateral amount x liquidation threshold); this rearrangement is derived here, not quoted from Aave. The same bound can be written as a tolerable price drop of 1 - 1/HF. (high confidence) — https://aave.com/help/borrowing/liquidations · keywords: Liquidation price math for looped positions · also: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08610
